newsitem.title: ROMANIA: 100,000 Romanian children in state institutions.
newsitem.headline: 100,000 Romanian children in state institutions.

text.p: Almost 100,000 Romanian children have been abandoned in state institutions and there is an urgent need to help them back into the community, a government official said on Friday.

"Statistics show we are faced with a disaster -- less and less children are born, while many newborn babies end up in institutions," Cristian Tabacaru, head of the government's child protection department, told a news conference. "If this doesn't stop, we'll face a bleak future."
For the first time since the 1989 fall of Communism, the government released official data on the number of children abandoned in state and private homes across the country.

Tabacaru said that by mid-May 1997, 98,872 children, up to 18 years of age, were living in some 650 orphanages, including 154 homes for abandoned children opened in the post-communist era and 73 homes run by local and foreign charities.
He said nearly 1,000 children had run away from those homes, with another 2,500 living on the streets of Bucharest and other big cities.
Romania, where living standards have plunged dramatically in the post-communist era, has one of the lowest birth rates and accounts for more than half of all juvenile AIDS cases in Europe.
Half of Romania's six million children live in families struggling to make ends meet, Tabacaru said.
Birth rates fell by 36 percent after the Communist-era ban on abortions was scrapped, and only 230,000 babies were born last year, down from 370,000 in 1989, he said.

The centrists, who toppled leftists in last November's elections, have called for international efforts to address the plight of an estimated one million children abandoned in post-communist institutions across eastern Europe.
Family breakdown and chronical unemployment were among reasons why many Romanian parents left their children in institutions, where orphans account for only 16 percent of the total, Tabacaru said.
"We must transfer responsibility for these children to the community, to families, relatives or foster parents," he said. "We must help these children to live a normal family life."
Romania, struggling with an austerity budget, has raised monthly child benefits to the equivalent of $7 now and has extended paid maternity leave for mothers or fathers to two years.
The government has also decided to give families taking care of an abandoned child an extra monthly bonus equivalent to $20. The average Romanian monthly wage is about $80.
